items.english: It was a heat such as had not been known for years. Wherever one looked, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses threw back the sunlight dull as lead, and the swallows' nests hung beneath them seemed, at this rate, like to steam the nestlings and the eggs within them alive. What was more, every field that was a field, whether of hemp or of millet, hung its head sodden in the reek of the earth, and there was not one but was wilted in its greenness. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken by the damp heat of these last days, was turbid and heavy near the ground though it was fair, and here and there mere shapes of towering cloud, like hail parched in an earthen pan, floated in clots. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who had gone out of their way to be in the blazing sun of a threshing-yard in such weather.
notes: Kept the hail parched in an earthen pan simile as written, though obscure: small hard lumps of cloud heated dry in a pan. It is bookish oddity, not to be smoothed away.
Kept wine worm as the fixed term for 酒虫, in quotes here to mark the borrowed tag.

items.english: Strangely, one of them lay naked, on his back on the bare ground. What was more, for some reason his hands and his feet were wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself showed no sign of minding it. He was short, fresh-coloured, somehow giving a sense of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stood at this man's pillow, though what might be inside that, too, was not to be known.
notes: hosobiki rendered as thin cord and suyaki no kame as unglazed jar, per bible, to keep the specifying texture. Kept fat as a pig low and unsoftened.

data.say: Drafted opening tableau in held past-tense stillness, keeping measures and low similes unsmoothed.
